splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions. This matters because it determines whether ambiguity in criminal provisions is resolved in favor of defendants or in favor of the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, meaning ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's anti-defendant interpretive commentary to control when the Guidelines text is ambiguous.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson, or instead impermissibly expands the guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and binding
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline entitled to deference under Stinson v. United States, and inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot expand the definition beyond the text, particularly after Kisor v. Wilkie narrowed the scope of deference to agency interpretations of their own rules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Courts are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision, which determines whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers or just one to be barred from safety-valve relief from mandatory minimums. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geographic location.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed on the federal schedule.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the career-offender and other guidelines provisions require that the substance underlying a state drug conviction also be controlled under federal law. This affects whether defendants with state marijuana or other drug convictions face significantly enhanced federal sentences.

positions.label: State law controls — no federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is also federally controlled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the underlying substance is also controlled under federal law, requiring a match between state and federal schedules.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: Cited in Henderson as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) (compassionate release).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law — such as the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory life sentences for certain drug offenses — can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. This affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences that would be lower if imposed today.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed through habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims, and whether habeas is available for such challenges.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement — including BOP decisions about prerelease custody under the First Step Act — must be brought as habeas petitions or may proceed as civil rights actions. The Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez and has not resolved it, leading to irreconcilable lower court decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is available to challenge conditions or terms of confinement, not just the fact or duration of imprisonment, giving prisoners a pathway to challenge BOP decisions about custody conditions.

positions.label: Habeas is limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and conditions-of-confinement claims must be brought through civil rights statutes like Bivens or § 1983.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to appeals from orders denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil deadline) or remains part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal deadline). This determines how long defendants have to appeal denials of fee requests.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline, representing the majority view.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion remains part of the criminal case and is subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Cited as minority view in Onamuti

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's assets belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A). This significantly affects debtors who convert in good faith but whose property has appreciated.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a), means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, purpose, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors in a good-faith conversion, noting that the contrary reading creates a circuit split.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Cited as opposing view in Castleman dissent

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust with the court.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether revocation of supervised release can be used to punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct, or whether the sentence at revocation must reflect only the breach of the court's trust. The Sixth Circuit allows express punishment for violations, placing it at the 'extreme' of a circuit split.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, allowing revocation sentences to reflect the severity of the underlying violation conduct.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must reflect breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release is primarily about sanctioning the breach of the court's trust, not punishing the defendant for the violation conduct itself, consistent with the Supreme Court's framework in Johnson v. United States.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Cited as opposing view in Esteras dissents

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries retain discretion to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined by the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select or adjust actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, giving plans flexibility to use more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, allowing courts to retain jurisdiction to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms and courts lack authority to extend the supervision period beyond what Congress specified in the statute.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits relitigating any previously presented claim — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims in § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have taken different approaches to whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures, with some circuits finding competitive injury sufficient and others requiring more concrete harm. The resolution affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when state laws change election rules in ways that could affect the outcome, allowing pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates must demonstrate more than speculative competitive harm to establish Article III standing for pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Cited in cert petition as opposing view

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment. This potentially conflicts with circuits that take a narrower view of the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical records qualify under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated after disclosure has occurred.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements and must await final judgment for appellate review.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Abdelhady as contrasting approach

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards to claims of discrimination in hospitality and business establishments, prompting SCOTUS review of the Second Circuit's approach. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide by establishing or refining standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing liability for discrimination or unfair treatment in business establishments, making it easier for plaintiffs to prevail.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a higher showing for claims of discrimination in business operations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
